In the FLD-first subgroup, multidisciplinary review was associated with management change (5/5 [100%] vs. 5/19 [26.3%], p = 0.0059). CONCLUSION: Sequential multimodality defecography changed management in approximately one-quarter of patients. Its value was greatest when MRD followed FLD, especially when examinations were performed closely together. MRD after FLD detected a higher frequency of second-test abnormalities, particularly cystocele. The association between multidisciplinary review and management change suggests that the clinical impact of sequential defecography depends not only on the added imaging findings but also on how they are integrated into treatment planning.

articles.title: End-to-end automated radiotherapy planning using transfer learning to overcome data scarcity.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To develop and benchmark 3D dose prediction algorithms for volumetric modulated arc therapy for head-and-neck (HN) and pancreatic cancer treatments, and to demonstrate the clinical feasibility of converting the predicted doses into deliverable plans. METHODS AND MATERIALS: Three deep learning models were pretrained on 3232 public plans and fine-tuned on institutional cohorts (256 HN and 72 pancreas patients). The accuracy of the fine-tuning strategy was compared with the baseline trained from scratch using only institutional data. In a prospective setting, the predicted dose was used as the planning goal for fully automated plan generation. Automated plans were benchmarked against clinical plans using Plan Quality Metrics. The deliverability of the fully automated plans was verified by Mobius ion-chamber patient-specific quality assurance (PSQA). RESULTS: Relative to training from scratch, transfer learning significantly accelerated convergence and minimized prediction error in scenarios with limited site-specific data. For HN cases, fine-tuning yielded a prediction error of 1.76 Gy. Notably, models fine-tuned on just 5% (n = 12) of the dataset achieved accuracy comparable to models trained from scratch using 50% (n = 116) of the training data. In the pancreas cohort, fine-tuning resulted in a mean absolute error of 1.35 Gy, representing a 14.6% reduction compared to the baseline trained solely on institutional data. When used for automated planning, these predicted 3D doses improved planning target volume homogeneity and organs at risk sparing (esophagus and trachea) in HN plans, while pancreas plans aimed to meet clinical goals with reduced dose to the spinal cord and right kidney. All automated plans were confirmed as clinically deliverable via PSQA. CONCLUSION: Compared with models trained from scratch on institutional data, transfer learning significantly reduced prediction error and improved robustness. The feasibility of converting predicted doses into clinical plans while maintaining plan quality through a fully automated process was demonstrated.

articles.title: Ultrashort Echo Time Magnetization Transfer MRI for Cortical Bone Collagen Assessment and Its Association With Mineralization in Type 1 Diabetes.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) increases fracture risk beyond bone mineral density (BMD), implicating matrix quality. Whether ultrashort echo time magnetization transfer (UTE-MT) MRI can track collagen alterations in T1DM and their associations with mineralization is unknown. PURPOSE: To evaluate UTE-MT-derived magnetization transfer ratio (MTR) for monitoring in vivo cortical collagen alterations in T1DM and to investigate its associations with mineralization and multiscale bone properties. STUDY TYPE: Longitudinal animal model. ANIMAL MODEL: 18 male New Zealand white rabbits (Age: 5-6 months) randomized to diabetic (n = 12) and control (n = 6) groups. FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: 3 T/3D gradient-echo UTE-MT sequence. ASSESSMENT: UTE-MT MRI was performed at baseline (week 0) and weeks 12, 16, and 20 post-alloxan induction. Cortical MTR was calculated from paired MT-on/off images and quantified over cortical regions of interest. Reference measurements at the terminal time point (week 20) included micro-CT (cortical porosity [CtPo]), histomorphometry (mineral apposition rate [MAR], bone formation rate [BFR/BS]), fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) (collagen cross-linking), liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) (hydroxyproline [Hyp]), histology (collagen maturation), and mechanical testing. STATISTICAL TESTS: The t-tests/Mann-Whitney U for endpoint cross-sectional comparisons, linear mixed-effects model for longitudinal MTR, Pearson correlations (r) for associations; p < 0.05 was considered significant. RESULTS: Cortical MTR declined in T1DM rabbits, becoming significantly lower than controls at week 12 and lowest at week 20. At termination, T1DM group demonstrated significantly higher CtPo (1.345 ± 0.270% vs. 0.591 ± 0.233%), elevated NE-xLR, reduced MAR, BFR/BS, Hyp, ECR, and collagen maturation (1.705 ± 0.548 vs. 5.474 ± 1.455). Mechanical properties (elastic modulus [E], yield strength [YS], toughness) were significantly lower in the T1DM group, with reductions of 44.1%, 35.2%, and 63.2% relative to controls, respectively. MTR at week 20 correlated positively with Hyp, ECR, collagen maturation, mineralization, and mechanical parameters (r = 0.562 to 0.900), and negatively with NE-xLR via partial correlation (r = -0.616) and CtPo (r = -0.826). DATA CONCLUSIONS: UTE-MT-derived MTR enables in vivo tracking of cortical collagen dynamics in T1DM. EVIDENCE LEVEL: 1. TECHNICAL EFFICACY: Stage 2.

articles.title: Practical considerations in measuring out-of-field neutron dose for pulsed and gantry-mounted proton therapy machines.
articles.abstract: Objective.Synchrocyclotrons deliver radiation in distinct macro pulses with high instantaneous dose rate that distinguish them from isochronous cyclotrons and synchrotrons. The relatively high instantaneous dose rates associated with synchrocyclotrons require special consideration in measurement of the neutron dose. The objective of this work is to measure the out-of-field neutron ambient dose equivalent (H*(10)) as a conservative operational surrogate to assess the fetal dose due to secondary neutrons for a gantry-mounted synchrocyclotron proton therapy system when an intensity modulated proton therapy (IMPT) brain treatment is delivered with the dynamic aperture (DA), static aperture (SA), and no aperture (NA).Approach.A pencil beam scanning (PBS) gantry-mounted synchrocyclotron was used for beam delivery. IMPT plans employing the DA, SA, and NA, each with 3 fields (vertex, lateral, and posterior-anterior (PA)) were optimized using the treatment planning system to treat a left-sided spherical brain target with 6 cm diameter to a total dose of 66 Gy (weighted by radiobiological effectiveness [RBE] 1.1) in 33 fractions. The plans were delivered to an anthropomorphic phantom and the neutron H*(10) was measured using two commercial rem-meters, a WENDI-II and a LUPIN-BF3-NP counter at 43, 53, 61, and 71 cm distance from the isocenter intended to mimic distances to a fetus at various gestational periods. To investigate the influence of the couch angle for the PA field, the neutron dose from the PA field was measured at several couch angles including 0°, 180°, and 270°.Main results.WENDI-II suffers from dead-time associated issues and underestimated the dose by a factor of ∼1.7-2.7 compared to LUPIN-BF3-NP. H*(10) showed dependence on the measurement location and the use of field shaping system. The total H*(10) for 66 Gy-equivalent proton dose was estimated to be 10.7 mSv (9.7 mSv) and 4.9 mSv (4.5 mSv) at 43 and 71 cm distance from the isocenter, respectively, when the SA (DA) was used. Without an aperture the corresponding values were 11.8 mSv and 5.3 mSv. The 270°-couch-angle resulted in the highest neutron dose from the PA field by ∼15% relative to the 0°-couch-angle, resulting in an increase in the neutron dose by ∼5% for the whole treatment.Significance.WENDI-II is not a reliable device for in-room neutron dose measurement for synchrocyclotrons with high instantaneous dose rates. Employing appropriate use of the aperture system as well as avoiding the 270° couch angle for the PA field can minimize the neutron dose in the gantry-mounted system studied in this work.

articles.title: Low-spatial-frequency perception enhancing dynamic convolutional network for system matrix recovery in magnetic particle imaging.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Magnetic particle imaging (MPI) is an emerging molecular imaging modality known for its high sensitivity and long-term tracking. System matrix (SM)-based image reconstruction is one of the most important reconstruction methods for MPI. However, MPI reconstruction based on the measured SM is limited by the requirement of voxel-stepwise precise calibration of system function within the field of view (FOV), which is time-consuming and noise-prone. Additionally, any changes in system properties require recalibrating the SM. This hinders the clinical translation and practical application of MPI. PURPOSE: To address these limitations, we propose a low-spatial-frequency perception enhancing dynamic convolutional network (LPEDCN) to recover SMs for accelerating calibration. METHODS: Specifically, we observe and reveal a positive correlation between the percentage of low-spatial-frequency energy and the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in the spatial Fourier transform (SFT) domain of real-world SM rows. Based on this prior, we design a low-spatial-frequency perception enhancement (LPE) joint loss to suppress high-frequency noise during model training. We also introduce a context-modulated dynamic convolution (CMDC) to capture long-range contextual features. We evaluate LPEDCN on simulated (training set: 60 SMs split into 107880 SM-row slices; validation set: 20 SMs split into 37520 slices; test set: 20 SMs split into 32660 slices; with no overlap between sets), public real-world OpenMPI (training set: 1 SM split into 101861 SM-row slices; validation set: 1 SM split into 62863 slices; test set: 1 SM split into 85347 slices; with no overlap between sets), and in-house (test set: 2 SMs split into 225 and 272 slices, respectively) datasets. SM recovery accuracy is evaluated by normalized root-mean-square error (nRMSE), and the reconstruction quality is evaluated by peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index measure (SSIM). We assess LPEDCN by comparing it with seven state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods. Statistical significance is evaluated using two-tailed t-tests with p < 0.05 after False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction, and practical significance is assessed using Cohen's d for effect size. RESULTS: LPEDCN not only accelerates SM calibration in MPI, but also exhibits higher accuracy in SM recovery and better quality in image reconstruction compared to SOTA methods. For the core SM recovery metric nRMSE, LPEDCN significantly outperforms SOTA methods (p < 0.05, FDR corrected) for 2×, 4×, and 8× super-resolution (SR), respectively, with effect size values of 0.23-1.02 on the simulated dataset and 0.06-45.63 on the public real-world OpenMPI dataset. For the image reconstruction metrics PSNR and SSIM, LPEDCN is significantly superior to SOTA methods (p < 0.05, FDR corrected) for 2×, 4×, and 8× SR, respectively, with effect size values of 0.45-8.68 on the simulated dataset, and 0.10-4.65 on the OpenMPI dataset. These quantitative results consistently verify that LPEDCN yields practically meaningful performance improvements. Additionally, LPEDCN greatly reduces the SM calibration time and achieves excellent high-resolution reconstruction images. CONCLUSION: LPEDCN holds practical promise for improving MPI calibration efficiency.

articles.title: Prediction of radiation-induced hypothyroidism after proton-based supraclavicular nodal irradiation in breast cancer.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The thyroid gland lies adjacent to the supraclavicular target and is highly radiosensitive, placing patients at risk for radiation-induced hypothyroidism (RIHT). While RIHT incidence and predictive models have been well described after photon-based irradiation, evidence in the proton therapy setting remains limited. PURPOSE: To evaluate the incidence of RIHT in breast cancer patients undergoing proton-based supraclavicular nodal irradiation and to develop proton-specific normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) models incorporating dose-volume, dose-averaged linear energy transfer (LETd)-volume, and dose-LETd-volume histogram (DLVH) metrics. METHODS: A total of 113 breast cancer patients treated with proton supraclavicular irradiation were retrospectively analyzed. Dose-volume, LETd-volume, and DLVH metrics were extracted for the thyroid gland and individual thyroid lobes. After exclusion of non-informative variables, univariable logistic regression models were developed for all retained candidate predictors. Internal validation and model selection were performed using 1000 bootstrap resamples, and the final bootstrap-selected predictor was defined as the variable with the highest selection frequency. Model performance was assessed using apparent and optimism-corrected area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Biological dose metrics were additionally generated using six published LET-dependent relative biological effectiveness (RBE) models and compared with the fixed-RBE model using paired DeLong tests. RESULTS: Seventeen patients (15.0%) developed RIHT after a median follow-up of 25 months (range, 9-80 months). Under the fixed-RBE framework, the final bootstrap-selected predictors were complementary DLVH metrics: CD10L2 (cc), denoting the absolute volume not simultaneously receiving dose ≥ 10 Gy(RBE) and LETd ≥ 2 keV/µm, CD35L3 (cc), and CD5L4 (cc) for the thyroid gland, ipsilateral lobe, and contralateral lobe, respectively. The corresponding apparent AUCs were 0.794, 0.763, and 0.817, with optimism-corrected AUCs of 0.738, 0.708, and 0.766, respectively. Among the LET-dependent RBE models, the Wedenberg model based on contralateral lobe CD10L4 (cc) yielded the numerically highest optimism-corrected AUC of 0.772. Although LET-dependent RBE models showed slightly higher apparent AUCs than the fixed-RBE model in some analyses, paired DeLong tests did not demonstrate statistically significant differences. CONCLUSIONS: RIHT is a clinically relevant toxicity after proton-based supraclavicular irradiation. Under the fixed-RBE framework, the optimal cutoff values for the final bootstrap-selected complementary DLVH predictors were 5.6 cc for thyroid gland CD10L2 (cc), 2.9 cc for ipsilateral lobe CD35L3(cc), and 4.3 cc for contralateral lobe CD5L4 (cc). Complementary DLVH metrics may be informative for RIHT risk prediction and support thyroid-aware optimization strategies in proton treatment planning, pending further validation.

articles.title: Convolutional neural network metal artifact reduction in ultra-high resolution photon counting detector CT of middle- and inner-ear implants.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Metallic inner- and middle-ear implants with submillimeter structures requiring ultra-high resolution (UHR) imaging invariably result in metal artifacts at CT, which can obscure adjacent microstructures and subtle pathologic findings. Current metal artifact reduction techniques can be less effective for small metal objects or metal in heterogeneous background anatomy, and can sometimes introduce new artifacts or noise. PURPOSE: To develop and evaluate an image-domain convolutional neural network to reduce metal artifacts near inner- and middle-ear implants in UHR photon-counting-detector (PCD)-CT. METHODS: For network training, three stapes prosthesis models containing titanium and platinum were randomly oriented within a head-sized phantom and imaged on a PCD-CT with a UHR protocol. Metal and metal+artifact images were isolated by subtraction of the phantom background followed by CT number thresholding. Isolated artifact signal was enhanced via multiplication with a randomized factor ranging from one to a pre-determined artifact amplification scalar hyperparameter. Paired training inputs (with artifacts) and labels (without artifacts) were created by adding metal-free patient temporal bone images with metal+artifact and metal images, respectively. Combinations of 9 patient CT volumes and 24 metal CT volumes were used to create 216 CT volumes for training and validation with an 80%/20% training/validation split. The network was retrained with different amplification scalars (5, 10, 20, 30, 40) and with either mean-squared-error or mean-absolute-error loss functions to determine the optimal combination of these hyperparameters. The network was tested on 7 CT volumes from patients with three different implant types: stapes prostheses, cochlear implants, and a transverse sinus stent. Network performance was quantified through the artifact index, noise magnitude, CT number preservation of metal and bone, and dimensions of metal measured as the full-width at half-maximum of CT number line profiles. RESULTS: Networks trained with mean-squared-error demonstrated a trade-off between metal artifact reduction and preservation of bone CT number as the artifact amplification scalar changed. The trade-off was not observed when mean-absolute error was used. Using the network with hyperparameters that best preserved bone and reduced artifacts simultaneously (mean-absolute-error, amplification scalar 20), the artifact index was improved by 83.2% (p < 0.001) across all implant types, and image noise was reduced by 46.8% (p < 0.001). Artifact reduction was significantly better for cases with stapes prostheses than the other implant types (p < 0.004), although artifact index was still greatly improved for all implant types (91.1% for the stapes prostheses, 81.3% for the CI, and 72.9% for the transverse sinus stent). Metal implant dimensions were not significantly different between the network input and output images (p = 0.67). CONCLUSION: An image-domain convolutional neural network with task-specific hyperparameters reduced artifact severity and image noise in UHR PCD-CT of different inner- and middle-ear implants without loss of fine image detail.

articles.title: Radial Tiny Golden Angle UTE (tyGA-UTE) for Cardiac MRI in the Small Animal Model.
articles.abstract: Robust cardiorespiratory motion correction is critical for high-quality ultra-high-field (UHF) preclinical cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Whereas radial tiny golden angle (tyGA) sampling, data-driven self-gating (sg), compressed sensing (CS), and ultrashort echo time (UTE) are individually well-established techniques, their integration into a unified acquisition and reconstruction pipeline, together with systematic validation at 11.7 T remains insufficiently explored. This study presents and validates a UHF-optimized tyGA-based UTE workflow that enables high-temporal-resolution sliding-window dynamic imaging (SW-tyGA-UTE) and high-spatial-resolution cardiorespiratory self-gated cine imaging (Gated-tyGA-UTE) from a single continuous acquired tyGA acquisition. All experiments were performed on an 11.7-T small-animal MRI system in 16 healthy wild-type mice. Cardiac functional parameters, image quality metrics (signal-to-noise ratio [SNR] and contrast-to-noise ratio [CNR]), and inter-/intra-observer reproducibility were systematically compared between the proposed tyGA-UTE pipeline and two navigator-gated reference techniques: retrospectively gated FLASH and UTE methodologies. SW-tyGA-UTE and Gated-tyGA-UTE reconstructions yielded global left ventricular functional parameters comparable to those obtained with the reference methods (all p > 0.05). All functional metrics showed excellent intra-observer (ICC = 0.94-0.99) and inter-observer (ICC = 0.90-0.98) reproducibility, with ejection fraction showing the highest measurement consistency. Image quality was evaluated using an image-based within-ROI noise quantification approach that captures both thermal noise and reconstruction-related artifacts. In this analysis, the Gated-tyGA-UTE protocol showed no statistically significant differences in left ventricular blood-pool SNR, myocardial SNR, or CNR relative to the reference sequences. In contrast, the high-temporal-resolution sliding-window reconstruction showed significantly reduced image quality across all three metrics, consistent with the expected spatiotemporal trade-off of undersampled dynamic imaging. This study validates a robust, UHF-optimized tyGA-UTE imaging workflow that generates both high-fidelity quantitative cine data and ultra-fast dynamic cardiac images from a single acquisition. The unified pipeline eliminates the need for sequential repeated scans, minimizes anesthesia-related physiological variability, and improves experimental efficiency, providing a practical tool for preclinical cardiac phenotyping, longitudinal studies, and drug screening.

articles.title: Association of Cardiac MRI-Derived Epicardial Adipose Tissue Index With Adverse Clinical Outcomes in Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The clinical relevance of the epicardial adipose tissue index (EATI) is increasingly recognized, but its association with clinical outcomes in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) remains inadequately investigated. PURPOSE: To evaluate the association between cardiac MRI-derived EATI and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with HFpEF. STUDY TYPE: Retrospective. POPULATION: Two hundred sixty-five patients with HFpEF (135 male; mean age 55 years). FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: 1.5 T/balanced steady-state free precession. ASSESSMENT: EATI was quantified on cardiac MRI cine images. MACE was defined as cardiac death or readmission for heart failure. STATISTICAL TESTS: Welch t-test or Mann-Whitney U test, Cox proportional hazards regression, Kaplan-Meier analysis with log-rank test, and global χ2 model comparison. A p value < 0.05 was considered significant. RESULTS: During a median follow-up of 33 months (22-65), 42 patients experienced MACE. EATI was significantly higher in the MACE group than in the no-MACE group (33.65 ± 13.91 vs. 26.13 ± 11.28 mL/m2, Z = -3.52, effect size r = -0.22). EATI was independently associated with MACE (multivariable HR = 1.04 [95% CI: 1.01-1.06]). Kaplan-Meier survival analysis confirmed that patients with low EATI had significantly higher event-free survival rate. A model combining EATI with other clinical and conventional imaging risk factors (χ2 = 42.3) showed significantly improved model discrimination for identifying patients at risk of MACE compared with models with clinical variables (χ2 = 26.0) or clinical and conventional imaging variables (χ2 = 34.3). DATA CONCLUSION: Cardiac MRI-derived EATI was independently associated with MACE in patients with HFpEF and showed favorable discriminatory performance compared with clinical and conventional imaging risk factors. EVIDENCE LEVEL: 3. TECHNICAL EFFICACY: Stage 5.

articles.title: Performance Analysis of Laplacian Re-Decomposition-Based PET-MRI Fusion for Quantitative Imaging Biomarkers in Alzheimer's Disease Classification.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Alzheimer's disease (AD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) represent critical stages along the continuum of cognitive decline. This study investigates the Laplacian Re-decomposition (LRD) method for fusing positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to develop a quantitative imaging biomarker for the classification of AD. MATERIAL AND METHOD: Data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database were used in this study. T1, T2, T2-FLAIR, and T2*-weighted MRI sequences, together with [18F]FDG-PET images, were preprocessed and fused using the LRD algorithm. Hippocampal and frontal lobe WM segmentation, performed via U-Net, enabled relative signal contrast (RSC) calculation as a quantitative biomarker for each modality and fused image. Fusion and segmentation performance were assessed using standard metrics. RSC statistically compared between diagnostic groups after adjustment for demographic confounds, and evaluated for classification performance using ROC/AUC analysis. RESULTS: The mean Dice coefficient achieved by the trained U-Net for hippocampus and frontal lobe WM segmentation were 0.93 and 0.95, respectively. ROC analysis revealed that the RSC extracted from T1-weighted images fused with PET outperformed other modalities for AD vs. Cognitively normal (CN) classification (AUC = 0.88, accuracy = 0.90). Also, T2-weighted images fused with PET, using RSC as a quantitative biomarker, achieved the best classification performance for AD vs. MCI (AUC = 0.81, accuracy = 0.81) and MCI vs. CN (AUC = 0.84, accuracy = 0.88) classification. CONCLUSION: Our findings indicate that RSC extracted from LRD-fused images achieves competitive classification performance, supporting its potential as a quantitative biomarker for AD.

articles.title: Habitat Radiomics and Machine Learning for Preoperative Three-class Classification of Pediatric Acute Appendicitis: A Dual-center Study with External Validation.
articles.abstract: Accurate preoperative differentiation of pediatric acute appendicitis subtypes is relevant to treatment planning. We developed and externally validated a machine-learning framework combining habitat-based computed tomography (CT) radiomics with clinical variables for three-class classification (simple, complex, and appendiceal abscess). This retrospective dual-center study included 317 children undergoing appendectomy at Institution A (training n = 222, internal validation n = 95) and 174 children at Institution B (external validation). K-means + + habitat segmentation (k = 3) of preoperative noncontrast CT volumes of interest yielded 1218 radiomic features; ten features selected on the training cohort were combined with 20 preoperative clinical variables. Eight classifiers were compared using macro-averaged one-versus-rest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), accuracy, and macro-F1, with bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs), DeLong tests, calibration statistics, and decision curve analysis. In external validation, naive Bayes achieved the highest macro-AUC (0.946, 95% CI 0.910-0.974), accuracy 0.776 (0.713-0.833), and macro-F1 0.766 (0.674-0.837), significantly exceeding all seven comparators among the configurations evaluated (p < 0.001); the internal validation macro-AUC was 0.940 (0.893-0.977). Per-class external AUCs were 0.920 (simple), 0.948 (complex), and 0.971 (abscess). Calibration slopes (0.23-0.30) indicated that probability outputs require recalibration before probabilistic use. In a five-arm ablation of the input feature blocks, the fusion model combining clinical variables with habitat radiomics performed best (external macro-AUC 0.971), ahead of habitat radiomics alone (0.952), clinical variables plus conventional whole-VOI radiomics (0.776), clinical variables alone (0.763) and conventional whole-VOI radiomics alone (0.582). Habitat radiomics combined with machine learning provided accurate, externally validated three-class classification of pediatric acute appendicitis in children undergoing appendectomy. Naive Bayes offered the most balanced subtype discrimination. The model is a subtype-stratification aid rather than a stand-alone diagnostic or treatment-selection tool.

articles.title: Training-Volume Analysis, Computational Efficiency, and Green AI in Rotator Cuff Calcific Tendinopathy Classification-A Two-Institution Study with External Validation.
articles.abstract: To evaluate how training data volume influences diagnostic performance, external validation, robustness to training-subset composition, and computational efficiency in a VGG19-based model for rotator cuff calcific tendinopathy (RCCT) classification on shoulder radiographs (XRs), using training data from a single development institution. This retrospective two-institution study included 5056 shoulder XRs. A Visual Geometry Group 19 (VGG19)-based pipeline was trained on four cumulative fractions of a 4268-XRs development cohort: 25% (M25), 50% (M50), 75% (M75), and 100% (M100), using stratified 5-fold cross-validation. To assess robustness to training-subset composition, three nested cumulative sampling realizations were generated for M25, M50, and M75, while M100 represented the fixed full-data reference. Models were evaluated on an internal test cohort ( n = 480  ) and an external validation cohort ( n = 308  ). Areas under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUCs) were compared using correlated DeLong tests with Holm adjustment. M75 and M100 were additionally assessed using two one-sided tests (TOST) with a ± 0.02  AUC equivalence margin. Training-volume robustness was assessed across repeated cumulative subset realizations. Grad-CAM localization was quantitatively evaluated against expert-defined lesion regions using Pointing Game, localization area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), and Energy-Based Pointing Game (EBPG), with Score-CAM used for qualitative corroboration. In the primary sampling realization, internal AUC increased from 0.869 with M25 to 0.951 with M100. External AUC increased from 0.835 (M25) to 0.903 (M50), 0.945 (M75), and 0.953 (M100). External improvements were significant from M25 to M50 and from M50 to M75 (both Holm-adjusted P < . 001  ), whereas the M75-to-M100 increment was small ( Δ AUC=0.008; P = . 161  ). M75 and M100 were externally equivalent within the ± 0.02  AUC margin (TOST P = . 016  ). Across three independently sampled M75 subsets, external AUC remained highly stable (0.945-0.948; mean ± standard deviation, 0.946 ± 0.001), and all three M75 realizations were equivalent to M100. Compared with M100, M75 required 11.4% less training time and 15.4% less measured energy. In the primary seed-42 realization, quantitative Grad-CAM localization generally improved with increasing training volume: M100 achieved the highest Pointing Game and localization AUPRC in both cohorts, whereas EBPG peaked at M75. Increasing training volume improved model discrimination, but external gains showed marked diminishing returns beyond M75 in this VGG19-based RCCT classification task. Near-maximal external performance at M75 was reproducible across independent training-subset realizations and statistically equivalent to full-data training within the evaluated margin, supporting training-volume analysis as a strategy for balancing performance and computational resources within this study setting. In this VGG19-based RCCT classification task using training data from a single development institution, external discrimination showed marked diminishing returns beyond 75% training volume, with highly reproducible M75 performance across independent subset realizations and statistical equivalence to full-data training within a ± 0.02  AUC margin.

articles.title: OCTA Vessel Segmentation via UNet Transformers and Deformable Receptive Fields: A Motion-Artefact-Resilient Deep Learning Framework.
articles.abstract: Optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) is a non-invasive medical imaging technique that helps doctors see the blood vessels of the retina and choroid in fine detail. However, OCTA images often suffer from motion artefacts, which lower the accuracy of vessel segmentation in the retina. In this paper, we propose V2Vnet, a robust volume-to-volume deep learning framework that combines a UNet transformer with deformable receptive fields (DRF) to overcome this problem. The transformer encoder captures the overall structure of the input volume and gathers multi-scale information about retinal blood vessels, while the DRF block makes the convolutional sampling grid more flexible by adding learnable two-dimensional offsets to the standard grid. Together, these components allow the network to detect and segment blood vessels accurately in motion-insensitive 3D OCT images from a single scan, removing the need for repeated acquisitions. We trained and evaluated V2Vnet on the public OCTA-500 dataset, and we further tested it on an independent retinal-layer parcellation dataset to check generalisation. Our proposed technique achieved an accuracy of 99.56 %  , an mIoU of 69.64 %  , an mDice of 79.14 %  , and an MSE of 0.0151 on 3D OCTA segmentation, outperforming UNet3D, UNETR, and IPNV2 across all metrics. Even when synthetic motion artefacts were introduced, V2Vnet still delivered the best mIoU and mDice scores. These results show that our framework is reliable, cost-effective, and well suited to clinical use, especially in low- and middle-income settings where multi-scan OCTA hardware may not be available.

articles.title: CAS-UNet: A Context-Adaptive Encoder-Decoder Network with Boundary-Distance Auxiliary Supervision for Histopathological Nuclei Segmentation.
articles.abstract: Histopathological nuclei segmentation is essential for quantitative pathological analysis but remains challenging due to staining variation, heterogeneous tissue backgrounds, diverse nuclear morphology, ambiguous boundaries, and the limited batch sizes commonly used for high-resolution image training. This study proposes CAS-UNet, a context-adaptive encoder-decoder framework with boundary-distance auxiliary supervision for binary nuclei-region segmentation. The proposed network integrates a Pathology-Adaptive Context Pyramid for adaptive multi-scale contextual aggregation, a Normalized Skip Selection Module for semantic-guided skip-feature filtering, a group-normalized residual decoder for feature reconstruction under small-batch settings, and Boundary-Distance Auxiliary Supervision for structural constraint learning. CAS-UNet was evaluated on five public histopathological nuclei datasets, including CoNIC, CPM17, MoNuSeg, NuInsSeg, and PanNuke. In the main benchmark comparison, CAS-UNet achieved the highest Dice and IoU values among the evaluated segmentation methods across the five datasets. Supplementary controlled experiments with five paired random seeds further demonstrated consistent improvements over U-Net and DeepLabV3+ under identical data partitions and training configurations. Additional experiments showed improved performance compared with traditional image-processing pipelines and more consistent segmentation results with Group Normalization than Batch Normalization under different batch sizes. Multi-seed component ablation experiments further characterized the contributions of PACP, NSSM, GN-based decoding, and BDAS. The proposed CAS-UNet provides an accurate and reliable framework for binary nuclei-region segmentation. Future work will focus on instance separation, stain-robust domain adaptation, independent clinical validation, and whole-slide image evaluation to further explore its potential for downstream pathological analysis.

articles.title: SynPAR for Empirical Membership Inference Auditing of Synthetic Radiomic and Embedding Data.
articles.abstract: To develop and evaluate SynPAR, a framework for reproducible membership-inference auditing and reporting of synthetic radiomic and embedding data. We evaluated feature releases from eight imaging cohorts using distance, density-ratio, and shadow-calibrated attacks. Reference-overlap experiments tested evaluation contamination. Graded exact-copy controls, with separate threshold-calibration and test records, measured discrimination and sensitivity at false-positive-rate (FPR) targets of 1%, 5%, and 10%. Findings informed a seven-item reporting checklist.  Reference overlap increased mean density-ratio area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUC) from 0.502 to 0.809 across five cohorts. Distance-shadow versus shadow-standardized density AUCs were 0.630 versus 0.523 for the conditional variational autoencoder and 0.584 versus 0.521 for the Wasserstein generative adversarial network; both diffusion implementations were near chance under distance-shadow testing. Across 380 controlled release conditions, sensitivity depended on copying fraction and operating point. With complete copying in independent normal-feature experiments, shadow-standardized density achieved AUC 0.967 but sensitivity 0.480 at rank-calibrated target 1% FPR (achieved 1.04%); distance achieved 1.000 for both, with achieved FPR 1.00%. SynPAR links reference checks and measured sensitivity to practical reporting recommendations. The findings support assessing discrimination and sensitivity to known exposure jointly at explicitly evaluated operating points when interpreting attack results.

articles.title: Reliability and Reproducibility of a Novel MRI-Based Classification System for Lumbar Intervertebral Disc Degeneration: A Comparative Study with the Pfirrmann Classification.
articles.abstract: This study assess the interobserver and intraobserver reliability of a novel eight-grade MRI-based classification system for lumbar intervertebral disc degeneration and fix it as describe its reproducibility relative to the five-grade Pfirrmann classification. In this retrospective single-center reliability study, 250 consecutive adults undergoing lumbar MRI between May 2025 and May 2026 were included, providing 1250 intervertebral discs from L1-L2 through L5-S1. Four blinded observers with different levels of musculoskeletal and spine imaging experience independently graded all discs using both classification systems. All assessments were repeated after a 3-week washout period with randomized image order. Overall interobserver agreement was assessed using quadratically weighted Gwet's AC2 and intraobserver agreement using quadratically weighted Cohen's kappa. Confidence intervals were calculated using patient-level cluster bootstrap resampling. Each classification generated 5000 grading assessments. At the initial assessment, interobserver Gwet's AC2 was 0.767 (95% CI 0.756-0.779) for the novel classification and 0.817 (95% CI 0.808-0.826) for Pfirrmann. Intraobserver weighted kappa ranged from 0.436 to 0.810 for the novel classification and from 0.507 to 0.833 for Pfirrmann. The novel eight-grade classification showed reproducible grading in this cohort, although its interobserver agreement was numerically lower than that of Pfirrmann and intraobserver agreement varied across readers. These findings do not establish clinical validity or statistical equivalence between the systems.

articles.title: Estimation of glomerular filtration rate by standard renal CT imaging.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To develop and evaluate a method to predict glomerular filtration rate (GFR) from clinical renal CT. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Medical records of adult living kidney donors operated between 2013 and 2022 and patients considered for neoadjuvant cisplatin prior to cystectomy between 2019 and 2024 were retrospectively reviewed. Inclusion criteria were (1) renal CT obtained at 100 or 120 kVp before and 5-15 min after contrast administration, and (2) iohexol clearance test within 2 months of imaging. The iohexol clearance test was performed on the same day as the cystatin C and creatinine measurements. Estimated GFR values included cystatin C-based eGFR (eGFRcystatin C), creatinine-based eGFR using the Cockcroft-Gault formula (eGFRCockcroft-Gault), and eGFR using the Revised Lund-Malmö formula (eGFRLMR18), which is based on both creatinine and cystatin C. Manual and automatic segmentations of the renal pelvis and bladder were performed in both the excretory and unenhanced phases. RESULTS: In total, 139 patients were included in the analysis (mean age 52 ± 13 years; 60% women). Multivariate linear regression analysis combining the segmentation-derived variable with body surface area and age gave an adjusted R-square of 0.77 to mGFRiohexol (p < 0.001). GFRCT had the strongest relationship to mGFRiohexol with a mean absolute error of 12.8 mL/min, compared with 15.6 mL/min for eGFRCockcroft-Gault, 14.2 mL/min for eGFRcystatin C, and 13.0 mL/min for eGFRLMR18. Manual and automatic segmentations had similar performance. Patients evaluated for cisplatin treatment had greater variation in CT-estimated split renal function than donors. CONCLUSION: Renal function can be estimated with high precision from clinical renal CT. KEY POINTS: Question Accurate GFR assessment is critical, but current methods are either labor-intensive or imprecise. Can renal CT imaging provide a reliable alternative? Findings CT-derived eGFR showed the strongest correlation with iohexol clearance (R² = 0.77), with lower error compared to creatinine- and cystatin C-based estimates. Critical relevance statement Routine CT imaging can provide precise estimates of kidney function, supporting donor evaluations, chemotherapy dosing, and critical care decisions when accurate renal function is essential.

articles.title: Coronary Flow Velocity Reserve by Stress Echocardiography: The Prognostic Key of Multiple Heart Diseases.
articles.abstract: Although evaluating coronary flow velocity reserve (CFVR) via stress echocardiography (SE) has been available for over three decades, its integration into routine clinical practice remains underutilized globally despite substantial technical and conceptual advances. A diminished CFVR serves as a potent predictor of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and all-cause mortality across a broad spectrum of cardiovascular diseases. Its prognostic value is particularly robust in epicardial coronary artery disease, heart failure, coronary microvascular dysfunction, nonischemic cardiomyopathies, metabolic disorders (e.g., diabetes mellitus and obesity), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, systemic autoimmune diseases, and cardiac allograft vasculopathy. This comprehensive narrative review details the technical methodology for interrogating resting and stress-induced coronary flow velocity (CFV) under physical and pharmacological protocols. Furthermore, it highlights the clinical applicability of CFVR by synthesizing single-center observational insights with evidence from large-scale multicenter registries, advocating for its broader adoption into diagnostic workflows to refine risk stratification and guide therapeutic management.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence for Thyroid Nodule Diagnosis: From Multimodal Integration to Clinical Utility.
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) for thyroid nodules should be evaluated against the decisions it changes, not diagnostic accuracy alone. This critical narrative review examines ultrasound, cytology, histology, and molecular models and distinguishes modality-specific prediction from implemented multimodal learning. The original PubMed/MEDLINE search through 10 August 2026 was supplemented on 25 September 2026 by targeted OpenAlex searches and checks of primary publications, reporting standards, and regulatory sources. Selected studies are compared by sample size, reference standard, acquisition setting, testing design, and performance with confidence intervals where available. We explain feature concatenation, intermediate representation learning, cross-attention, and decision-level fusion, and examine whether integration improves on the strongest component. Reported gains are inconsistent, and complete-case multimodal datasets may exclude the low-risk nodules most relevant to avoiding biopsy. High discrimination for histological malignancy or occult nodal disease does not demonstrate reduced overdiagnosis, fewer operations, or improved survival. A thyroid-specific translation roadmap therefore addresses active surveillance, partial verification and spectrum bias, Hashimoto thyroiditis and multinodular disease, cytology preparation shifts, category-specific thresholds, operator dependence, reporting frameworks, and regulatory change control. The priority is a calibrated, externally tested tool using information available at a defined clinical decision, followed by prospective evaluation of patient and workflow outcomes. A unified imaging-pathology-omics system and reliable AI prediction of surveillance progression remain research objectives rather than established clinical capabilities.

articles.title: Influenza in Pregnancy: From the Maternal Lung to the Placenta and Fetus.
articles.abstract: Influenza in pregnancy is associated with a higher risk of severe respiratory disease and adverse maternal and perinatal outcomes, particularly later in gestation. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on epidemiology, pathophysiology, placental and fetal consequences, clinical presentation, diagnosis, antiviral management, and vaccination. Pregnancy involves dynamic immune adaptation together with reduced respiratory reserve, increased oxygen consumption, and cardiovascular changes that may amplify the effects of influenza pneumonia. Placental and fetal consequences appear to be mediated predominantly by maternal hypoxemia, fever, systemic inflammation, and hemodynamic disturbance; transplacental viral transmission is rare. Therefore, adverse fetal and neonatal outcomes are more closely linked to the severity and timing of maternal illness, placental dysfunction, and prematurity than to direct fetal infection. Prompt recognition is essential, and antiviral treatment should not await laboratory confirmation when influenza is suspected. Oseltamivir remains the preferred antiviral therapy and should be initiated as early as possible, including in patients presenting after 48 h with progressive or severe disease. Seasonal inactivated or recombinant influenza vaccination is the cornerstone of prevention, protecting both the mother and the infant through transplacental transfer of influenza-specific IgG. This integrated perspective supports vaccination, early diagnosis, and timely treatment to reduce maternal and perinatal risk.

articles.title: From Divergent Pathogenesis to Precision Medicine: The Road to Targeted Therapy in HIV-Associated and HIV-Unrelated Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma.
articles.abstract: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common and biologically heterogeneous subtype of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. While immunochemotherapy has improved outcomes, survival remains variable due to substantial molecular diversity. In people living with HIV (PLWH), DLBCL is the predominant lymphoma subtype and demonstrates more aggressive clinical behaviour, characterised by advanced-stage disease, extranodal involvement, and a potentially poorer prognosis despite antiretroviral therapy. Clarifying differences in the pathogenesis of HIV-associated and HIV-unrelated DLBCL is essential for informing precision therapies. This narrative review highlights the contrasting pathogenic mechanisms, with an emphasis on the interplay between viral oncogenesis, host immunity, and molecular alterations in HIV-associated DLBCL versus DLBCL in immunocompetent individuals. Understanding these differences is critical for refining diagnostic approaches, improving risk stratification, and identifying novel therapeutic strategies tailored to both groups.

articles.title: Reference Standards in Artificial Intelligence Detection of Apical Periodontitis: A Narrative Review of What Reported Accuracy Measures.
articles.abstract: The accuracy reported for detecting apical periodontitis using artificial intelligence (AI) is generally interpreted as accuracy against the disease; however, this is usually not the case. Compared with histopathology, single-view periapical radiography detects 16 to 27% of confirmed lesions and 38% with parallax, with a pooled digital sensitivity of 61.0% and a negative predictive value of 41.6%. Two blinded specialists reading 1717 radiographs disagreed on 22% of teeth. Detection depended on lesion size and site: simulated cancellous-bone lesions were invisible below 1 mm in incisors and 3 mm in molars. Of the 44 primary studies identified, 34 (77%) used a label that was a reading of the index image or was unascertainable; eight (18%) used an independent reference-six (14%) suited to contemporaneous detection and two to later treatment outcomes. No cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) input study had a reference independent of its volume. One commercial platform reported 92.3% sensitivity against same-image consensus and 47.9% against blinded CBCT. The reported accuracy is thus in agreement with a noisy rater; recognising this changes what meta-analyses pool. A model that reproduces human labels would have a lower sensitivity against disease than reported; for real-world models, the direction depends on error dependence that the study design cannot identify.

articles.title: Handheld Ultrasound: Technical Review and International Expert Consensus Recommendations.
articles.abstract: Background: Handheld ultrasound (HHUS) is increasingly used in point-of-care imaging because of its portability, accessibility, versatility, and comparatively low cost. Methods: This structured narrative technical review evaluated current HHUS technology, image quality and functionality, clinical applications, regulatory considerations, and future perspectives using recent literature, comparative studies, technical sources, and previous EFSUMB/WFUMB position papers. A structured SWOT analysis informed draft recommendations, which underwent three rounds of scientific discussion and revision by a 17-member international multidisciplinary expert panel. Each of the seven final recommendations was subsequently voted on separately, with consensus predefined as ≥80% agreement. Results: While HHUS devices are increasingly suitable for routine clinical use, further standardization, clinician training, and regulatory alignment are essential for widespread adoption. Conclusions: HHUS can expand access to focused ultrasound imaging, particularly in point-of-care and resource-limited settings. Its appropriate use requires task-specific device selection, adequate training, quality assurance, and recognition of its limitations compared with comprehensive ultrasound systems.

articles.title: Skene's Gland Malignancy from Imaging Diagnosis to Management: A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Skene's gland malignancies are extremely rare tumors of the female paraurethral region, known almost exclusively from case reports and small case series. Their diagnosis is often delayed because symptoms are nonspecific and may mimic benign periurethral disorders, urethral diverticula, primary urethral carcinoma or anterior vaginal wall tumors. This narrative review focuses on the role of imaging, particularly pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), in the diagnosis, differential diagnosis, staging and treatment planning of Skene's gland malignancies, distinguishing evidence from confirmed Skene's gland cases from evidence extrapolated from female urethral carcinoma. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science were searched on 27 September 2026 (publication years 2015-2026) and supplemented by reference-list screening; an explicit case definition was applied. Results: Of 191 records (93 after de-duplication), 17 reports of Skene's gland malignancy were included (15 case reports or series and 2 systematic reviews); fewer than thirty cases have been published overall. Patients were mostly postmenopausal (median age about 70 years, range 45-91), presenting with an asymptomatic periurethral nodule, hematuria or vaginal bleeding, or lower urinary tract symptoms; no uniform staging system has been applied. Most tumors were prostatic-type adenocarcinomas treated by local excision alone; radiotherapy, chemotherapy or androgen deprivation were used mainly for nodal, metastatic or recurrent disease. After examination, ultrasonography can detect and characterize a paraurethral mass, whereas MRI best defines tumor epicenter, urethral, periurethral and anterior vaginal wall involvement and regional spread, and should precede cystourethroscopy and biopsy; CT and PET/CT are complementary for systemic staging. No single immunohistochemical marker establishes Skene's gland origin. Conclusions: MRI is central to localizing and staging suspected Skene's gland malignancy and thus to guiding biopsy and the choice between local excision and radical surgery, but most imaging recommendations are extrapolated from female urethral carcinoma and require validation in pooled multicenter data.

articles.title: Diagnostic Communication and the Care That Follows: A Critical Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: An accurate diagnosis does not ensure that a patient understands its implications or receives appropriate care. This critical narrative review draws on purposively selected literature studies on diagnostic labels, explanations of test results, nocebo effects and care after diagnostic revision. Terminology experiments show changes in perceived severity and stated preferences, often in hypothetical settings. Clinical effects on symptoms and healthcare use depend on the intervention, comparator and outcome; explanation is frequently combined with treatment changes. Nocebo experiments demonstrate possible symptom mechanisms, not the cause of an individual patient's continuing symptoms. Studies of diagnostic follow-up identify a separate problem: accurate or revised findings may fail to inform subsequent care. The synthesis distinguishes evidence for changing understanding, relieving symptoms and completing appropriate clinical action. A documented misunderstanding or obsolete instruction can warrant correction while symptom assessment continues. Evaluation should measure accurate understanding, informed choices and care received, with symptoms assessed separately. Truthful disclosure and follow-up remain responsibilities even when symptom benefit is uncertain.

articles.title: The Human Labial Superficial Musculoaponeurotic System (SMAS): Anatomy, Imaging, and Biomechanical and Sensory Implications-A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: The superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) is a fundamental concept in facial anatomy and surgery, but its organization within the human lips remains incompletely defined. This narrative review critically reassesses the anatomical evidence for a labial SMAS and its regional configuration. Published anatomical, histological, and imaging evidence was critically reviewed. The literature review is complemented by original qualitative histological and imaging observations of the human lips, included exclusively for morphological correlation with the published anatomical evidence and not as an independent quantitative study. The available evidence does not demonstrate a classical, readily separable laminar SMAS within the lips. Instead, it supports a three-dimensional connective tissue network extending from the oral mucosa to the skin and intimately incorporating the orbicularis oris muscle. This organization is associated with neurovascular structures and may have biomechanical and sensory implications, although these functional interpretations are not directly demonstrated by the present material. The labial connective tissue architecture differs from the classical laminar SMAS described in other facial regions and may represent its regional equivalent. Further three-dimensional anatomical studies are required to establish this interpretation conclusively. By defining the normal fibromuscular architecture of the lips and the limits of its visualization, this review provides an anatomical framework for interpreting lip imaging while emphasizing that a labial SMAS is not currently a validated diagnostic or prognostic marker.

articles.title: Occult Neoplasms in Sudden Unexpected Death in Infancy: A Scoping Review of Post-Mortem Findings.
articles.abstract: Background: Sudden unexpected death in infancy (SUDI) may occasionally be attributable to neoplasms that were clinically unrecognised before the terminal event and diagnosed or confirmed during post-mortem investigation. These occult neoplasms are exceptionally rare and remain poorly characterised. This scoping review identifies published reports of neoplasms not diagnosed or strongly suspected before the terminal event in infants who died suddenly and unexpectedly, and systematically collects data on pathological features, diagnostic modalities, mechanisms of death, and the extent to which the neoplasm contributed to death. Methods: A search of PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus was conducted without a lower publication-date restriction through 19 July 2026, in accordance with Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and PRISMA-ScR. Publications describing sudden unexpected deaths in infants younger than 12 months with a previously undiagnosed neoplasm were selected and reviewed. Findings were extracted, and deaths were classified according to whether the neoplasm was causal, contributory, or incidental to death. Results: Twenty-five studies comprising 32 infant cases were included in the review. The median age at death was 2.5 months. The most frequent lesions were cardiovascular or thoracic neoplasms (16/32), followed by haematological or lymphoid neoplasms (6/32). Sixteen lesions were benign, ten were malignant, and six were intermediate, uncertain, or tumour-like. Twenty-five neoplasms were evident on macroscopic examination, whereas seven were identified only histologically. Reported mechanisms of death included arrhythmia, mechanical obstruction, respiratory failure, haemodynamic compromise, haemorrhage, leukostasis, and diffuse infiltration. Within the published cases included in this review, the review team classified the neoplasm as causal in 16 cases (16/32, 50.0%), contributory in 13 cases (13/32, 40.6%), and incidental in three cases (3/32, 9.4%). Conclusions: Autopsy examination is critical for identifying previously undiagnosed neoplasms, which are rare but potentially important findings in the investigation of SUDI. Among the selected published cases included in this review, the review team classified the neoplasm as causal in half of cases; this proportion should not be extrapolated to the broader SUDI population. Comprehensive autopsy assessment of SUDI cases, including thorough histological sampling and ancillary testing, is therefore essential for determining the role of a tumour in infant death.

articles.title: The Least Understood Placental Galectins: Galectin-14 and Galectin-16 in Human Pregnancy and Placental Biology.
articles.abstract: Galectins represent a family of proteins which are capable of specifically binding to beta-galactoside-containing sugar molecules, known as glycans. Galectins possess carbohydrate recognition domains (CRDs) that fundamentally determine their ability to bind to sugars. Galectin-14 (Gal-14) and galectin-16 (Gal-16) are members of the galectin family that is particularly associated with the placenta. The galectins in the placenta constitute a specialized subgroup functioning at the maternal-fetal interface. They are expressed primarily in the syncytiotrophoblasts. This trophoblast layer is in direct contact with maternal blood and plays a crucial role in the metabolic, hormonal and immunological interactions between the fetus and the pregnant woman. In order to prepare this structured narrative review, we conducted a structured literature search across the MEDLINE (PubMed), Embase, Cochrane Library and Web of Science Core Collection databases; the final search has been performed on 1 July 2026. The search strategy has combined the terms galectin-14/LGALS14 and galectin-16/LGALS16 with terms related to the placenta, trophoblast, pregnancy, placentation and pregnancy complications. Search results were imported into Mendeley Reference Manager to remove duplicates, and the reference lists of relevant review articles and studies were manually screened. Two reviewers (Z.K. and A.S.) independently screened the titles and abstracts and subsequently evaluated the potentially relevant full-text articles. The final evidence synthesis included primary studies that directly investigated the expression, function, regulation, or clinical associations of LGALS14 or LGALS16; secondary publications were used for background and contextual information. In experimental studies, galectin-14 has been linked to trophoblast migration and invasion-involving mechanisms such as the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway, MMP-9 and N-cadherin-as well as to the modulation of activated maternal immune cell function. Galectin-16 is structurally more distinct and exhibits reduced classical β-galactoside-binding capacity; it appears to be closely associated with trophoblast differentiation and syncytialization, presumably through intracellular protein interactions. Altered expression of placenta-specific galectins has been observed in preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction; however, the causal relationship remains unclear. Clinical evidence regarding their use as biomarkers is emerging at this time; therefore, neither galectin-14 nor galectin-16 can be currently considered as a validated, clinically applicable biomarker. Altogether, available evidence mandates further study of galectin-14 and galectin-16, as they may be important regulators of placental biology and potential biomarker candidates. However, their physiological functions and clinical utility have not yet been sufficiently confirmed; therefore, further prospective and functional studies are required. The strongest putative mechanistic link to the development of preeclampsia exists for galectin-14, primarily involving trophoblast migration and invasion as well as PI3K/Akt-related signaling pathways. In contrast, evidence in connection with the direct role of galectin-16 is limited at present.

articles.title: Gastrointestinal Involvement in Pediatric Behçet's Disease: A Focused Analysis from a Comprehensive Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Background: Gastrointestinal (GI) involvement is a clinically relevant but still incompletely characterized manifestation of pediatric Behcet's disease (PedBD). This systematic review provides a focused analysis of GI involvement in PedBD (addressing its frequency, clinical symptomatology, anatomical/endoscopic features, and therapeutic management) as a dedicated sub-analysis of a broader systematic review. Methods: A systematic search of MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, CENTRAL, and ClinicalTrials.gov was conducted, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Observational studies reporting GI involvement in patients with PedBD (disease onset before 16 years of age) were included, and data on frequency, symptoms, anatomical/endoscopic findings, and treatment of GI-PedBD were extracted and synthesized. Results: Thirty studies were included. Most studies were not focused on GI manifestations in PedBD as a (primary) study aim. The frequency of GI involvement ranged widely across the selected articles with a median of approximately 15% among studies with ≥50 pediatric BD patients. Abdominal pain and diarrhea were the most consistently reported symptoms. Endoscopic data indicated frequent involvement of the ileocecal region and terminal ileum, with mucosal ulcers and erosions as the predominant findings. Therapeutic data specific to GI-PedBD were limited to two studies only. As an appendix to the systematic review in the discussion, relevant case reports were described: anti-TNF agents, particularly adalimumab, showed favorable outcomes in refractory cases. Conclusions: GI involvement in PedBD is not negligible and can be severe. Its clinical and endoscopic characterization remains incomplete due to substantial heterogeneity in reporting practices across studies. Anti-TNF agents may represent an effective therapeutic option, especially for refractory GI-PedBD. Prospective and multicenter studies with standardized GI assessment protocols are needed to better characterize this clinically relevant subgroup of PedBD patients.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence in Gastroenterology: Towards Explainable, Generalisable and Clinically Actionable Decision Support.
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in gastroenterology for endoscopic detection and characterisation, disease-activity assessment, risk prediction, treatment-response estimation and workflow support. However, high retrospective accuracy does not necessarily translate into reliable or beneficial clinical decision support. This structured narrative review examines the clinical development of artificial intelligence across gastrointestinal endoscopy, inflammatory bowel disease, hepatology and pancreaticobiliary diseases through three translational dimensions: explainability, generalisability and clinical actionability. Communication, human oversight and lifecycle governance are considered cross-cutting determinants of implementation. The evidence is most mature in gastrointestinal endoscopy, particularly for computer-aided polyp detection, although benefits vary across operators, indications and practice settings. Applications in inflammatory bowel disease, hepatology and pancreaticobiliary care remain predominantly retrospective, with limited prospective evidence that model outputs alter management or improve patient outcomes. Explainability is commonly represented by heatmaps or feature-attribution methods, but rarely evaluated in terms of clinician understanding, calibrated trust or patient communication. External validation is becoming more frequent, yet geographic and technological transportability, calibration and performance under dataset shift remain insufficiently assessed. Prospective implementation and health-economic studies are uncommon, and available economic evidence is largely model-based. Clinical artificial intelligence should therefore be evaluated as a sociotechnical intervention comprising the model, interface, users, workflow, communication process and associated care pathway. Translation requires clinically defined use cases, representative multicentre validation, human-centred evaluation, prospective assessment of benefits and harms, and continuous post-deployment surveillance. Clinical AI in gastroenterology should complement clinical expertise through transparent, contestable and continuously monitored decision support that preserves clinician accountability and supports informed, patient-centred decisions.

articles.title: Effects of Dialysate Calcium Concentration on Bone, Mineral Metabolism, and Vascular Outcomes in Maintenance Hemodialysis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: The optimal dialysate calcium concentration in maintenance hemodialysis remains uncertain because reducing calcium exposure may limit calcium loading but can also stimulate parathyroid hormone secretion and impair intradialytic cardiovascular stability. We evaluated randomized evidence across bone, mineral metabolism, vascular, and acute safety outcomes. Methods: PubMed, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and Scopus were searched from database inception through 10 July 2026, with targeted citation and publication-status updating through 1 August 2026. Randomized parallel, crossover, factorial, and multi-period trials comparing dialysate calcium concentrations in adults receiving hemodialysis or hemodiafiltration were eligible. Acute and chronic outcomes were analyzed separately. Pooled estimates used inverse-variance random-effects models with DerSimonian-Laird estimation and modified Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals. Results: Twenty-four randomized parent trials were included. Lower dialysate calcium reduced end-of-dialysis ionized calcium (paired mean difference, -0.193 mmol/L; 95% CI, -0.258 to -0.128), with substantial heterogeneity. Point estimates for chronic parathyroid hormone and total alkaline phosphatase were higher and serum calcium lower, but all confidence intervals crossed the null. No clear effects were demonstrated for phosphate, calcium-phosphate product, lumbar bone mineral density, coronary artery calcification, or carotid intima-media thickness. Acute parathyroid hormone, blood pressure, calcium-balance, and QTc estimates suggested greater parathyroid stimulation, lower hemodynamic measures, less calcium gain, and longer QTc with lower calcium, but were imprecise. Adverse events were unsuitable for pooling. Conclusions: Lower dialysate calcium consistently lowers postdialysis ionized calcium, but its long-term skeletal and vascular effects remain uncertain. No single concentration appears universally optimal; prescription should be individualized according to mineral metabolism phenotype, cardiovascular tolerance, dialysis modality, and concomitant therapy.

articles.title: Detection Strategies for HER2 and miR-21 in Breast Cancer: Current Approaches and Future Perspectives- Hybrid Systematic Review and Bibliometric Mapping.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Breast cancer is still one of the main causes of mortality and morbidity at a global level, highlighting the need to identify robust biomarkers for early diagnosis, prognostic stratification and optimization of therapeutic decisions. Among these biomarkers, HER2 (Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2) and miR-21 represent the complementary levels of tumor biology, reflecting oncogenic signaling at the protein level and post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression. This hybrid systematic review and bibliometric mapping aims to critically analyze current methods for determining HER2 and miR-21 biomarkers, highlighting their advantages, limitations and clinical applicability, as well as future development directions in the field of precision oncology diagnostics. Methods: The bibliometric analyses were performed to investigate the intellectual structure, research trends, and collaboration patterns within the field of HER2 and miR-21 detection in breast cancer. A PRISMA-guided literature search was conducted in the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC), PubMed, and Scopus. After duplicate removal, screening, and eligibility assessment, 305 publications were included in the final review corpus. Bibliometric analyses of these 305 publications were performed using VOSviewer to investigate publication output, keyword co-occurrence, co-authorship, and institutional and country collaboration patterns. Results: Bibliometric analyses revealed the intellectual structure, research trends, and collaboration patterns within the field of HER2 and miR-21 detection in breast cancer. This work highlights the complementary role of HER2 and miR-21 biomarkers in breast cancer, highlighting their fundamental differences, but also their synergistic potential in clinical practice and translational research. A comparative analysis of detection methods highlights that, although conventional techniques remain the clinical standard, they are increasingly complemented by advanced technologies, such as digital PCR, optical and electrochemical biosensors. Conclusions: The emerging detection methods offer significant advantages in terms of sensitivity, rapidity and potential for miniaturization, but their clinical implementation is still limited by the lack of standardization and large-scale validation. A major bibliometric insight is the evident shift in publication output by country toward Asia, particularly China, India, and Iran, which currently show high publication output and extensive collaborative connectivity in the analyzed network. However, challenges remain in standardizing microRNA methods and the clinical validation of emerging technologies.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Medical Diagnosis in the Internet of Medical Things: An End-to-End Survey of Connected Sensing, Distributed Intelligence, Clinical Applications, and Validation.
articles.abstract: The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) can extend diagnostic observation beyond episodic encounters by connecting wearable, point-of-care, imaging, and bedside devices to artificial-intelligence services. Yet continuous measurement is not itself diagnosis: a clinically useful system must establish signal validity, map an output to a defined diagnostic role, communicate uncertainty, and demonstrate agreement with an appropriate reference standard. This survey analyzes the complete IoMT diagnostic pathway from acquisition and quality control through edge-fog-cloud computation, machine and deep learning, federated training, and clinician-governed action. It distinguishes monitoring, screening, early detection, differential diagnosis, prognosis, and decision support because these tasks require different labels, thresholds, metrics, and evidence. Evidence is synthesized across electrocardiography and cardiovascular risk, glucose and metabolic assessment, connected imaging and oncology, respiratory and infectious-disease detection, electroencephalography and seizure recognition, and decentralized point-of-care testing. The analysis shows how sensor placement, missingness, compression, latency, privacy mechanisms, and site heterogeneity can change diagnostic performance even when the model is unchanged. A diagnostic evidence framework is therefore proposed that links reference standards and patient-level data separation to sensitivity, specificity, calibration, external validation, target-device feasibility, uncertainty-based referral, and prospective workflow utility. Security, explainability, and lifecycle monitoring are treated as conditions of diagnostic reliability rather than independent features. The resulting synthesis provides a clinically centered basis for deciding which IoMT outputs may support screening or diagnosis, which remain monitoring signals, and what evidence is still required before deployment.

articles.title: Robotic-Assisted Bronchoscopy for Peripheral Pulmonary Lesions: Current Evidence, Clinical Applications, and Future Directions.
articles.abstract: The evaluation of peripheral pulmonary lesions (PPLs) is a persistent clinical challenge, made more pressing by the expansion of low-dose CT lung cancer screening. Conventional and earlier navigational bronchoscopy, including electromagnetic navigation, historically achieved diagnostic yields of approximately 60-70%, with CT-to-body divergence contributing to nondiagnostic sampling. This narrative review, prepared using the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA), summarizes robotic-assisted bronchoscopy (RAB) platform technology, procedural optimization, diagnostic performance, safety, molecular tissue adequacy, and emerging applications. A structured search was updated through September 2026; this is not a systematic review. Using the strict definition recommended by the American Thoracic Society/American College of Chest Physicians (ATS/ACCP), the most comprehensive meta-analysis reported a pooled RAB diagnostic yield of 69.6%, while the prospective multicenter TARGET study reported an adjudicated strict yield of 61.6%. Higher pooled estimates of approximately 84-87% generally use intermediate definitions that the ATS/ACCP statement recommends against as primary diagnostic-yield measures. RAB pneumothorax rates are approximately 2% in pooled analyses, compared with approximately 20-25% for CT-guided transthoracic needle biopsy. In the randomized RELIANT trial, RAB was non-inferior, but not superior, to electromagnetic navigation bronchoscopy; in VERITAS, navigational bronchoscopy as a category was non-inferior to transthoracic needle biopsy for 12-month diagnostic accuracy, with fewer pneumothoraces. RAB is a useful option for selected PPLs, but strict-definition performance is more modest than frequently quoted intermediate yields. Outcomes depend on lesion characteristics, sampling strategy, operator experience, center volume, and imaging infrastructure.

articles.title: Multimodality Imaging in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: From Phenotyping to Precision Clinical Management.
articles.abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a genetically and phenotypically heterogeneous myocardial disease characterized by unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy and a broad spectrum of clinical manifestations, ranging from an asymptomatic phenotype to heart failure, atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, sudden cardiac death, and advanced heart failure. Accurate diagnosis and risk stratification therefore require complex assessment. Multimodality cardiovascular imaging provides complementary structural, functional, and tissue characterization that cannot be obtained using a single imaging technique. Transthoracic echocardiography remains the cornerstone of initial diagnosis, hemodynamic assessment, and longitudinal follow-up, while advanced echocardiographic techniques provide additional information regarding myocardial and left atrial mechanics. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) has become central to phenotypic characterization and tissue assessment. Cardiac computed tomography offers complementary high-resolution anatomical information, particularly for coronary assessment and procedural planning, whereas nuclear imaging, provides insights into coronary microvascular dysfunction, myocardial perfusion, and selected phenocopies such as transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis. Multimodality imaging also facilitates differentiation of HCM from other conditions such as athlete's heart, hypertensive heart disease, and infiltrative cardiomyopathies. Integration of imaging biomarkers with clinical and genetic information may improve prediction of adverse outcomes. Thus, multimodality imaging should be regarded not as a collection of competing techniques but as an integrated framework for precision diagnosis, risk stratification, therapeutic planning, and longitudinal management of patients with HCM.

articles.title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging in Axial Spondyloarthritis: Beyond the Sacroiliac Joints-Focus on Facet Joint Involvement.
articles.abstract: Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) is a chronic inflammatory disease of the sacroiliac joints (SIJs) and spine, encompassing non-radiographic axSpA (nr-axSpA) and radiographic axSpA (r-axSpA) or ankylosing spondylitis (AS). Early diagnosis is challenging, particularly in nr-axSpA, due to the absence of radiographic sacroiliitis and overlap with nonspecific back pain. Imaging plays a pivotal role in disease classification and monitoring. To synthesize current evidence on inflammatory and structural facet joint involvement in axSpA, with particular emphasis on MRI characterization, available scoring approaches, differentiation from degenerative abnormalities, and the current limitations of facet joint assessment as a potential imaging biomarker. A review of current evidence regarding imaging modalities in axSpA, including conventional radiography, computed tomography (CT), MRI, radionuclide techniques, and musculoskeletal ultrasound (US), was performed. Particular emphasis was placed on ASAS/OMERACT MRI definitions and facet joint assessment. MRI enables early detection of inflammatory lesions such as bone marrow edema (BME), spondylitis, and enthesitis before structural damage becomes visible on radiographs. It also identifies structural changes including fat metaplasia, erosions, syndesmophytes, and ankylosis. Increasing evidence supports the clinical relevance of facet and costovertebral joint inflammation, which correlates with impaired spinal mobility and functional disability. However, inflammatory facet joint changes remain underreported in routine practice despite the development of semiquantitative scoring systems.
